screens.title: Automating System Initialization with systemd tools
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn practical, hands-on techniques to inspect and improve system startup. We start with systemd-analyze to measure boot time, find slow units with blame, and reveal the critical path with critical-chain. Then you will learn how to capture a visual timeline with systemd-bootchart so you can see which units run in parallel, which block others, and where idle waits occur. Armed with that evidence, you'll practice a targeted troubleshooting workflow: identify suspects, inspect logs, test unit files, and apply dependency and resource changes that shorten the critical path. Finally, you'll automate post-boot activities by writing a Type=oneshot service that runs after multi-user and network-online targets, and learn unit-level best practices like Restart policies, cgroup limits, and pre-flight checks. These techniques let you ensure critical services start reliably, reduce boot time, and automate necessary system health checks. By the end you will be able to both diagnose boot bottlenecks and create dependable automation that runs at the right time during startup.

This practice helps you avoid common mistakes: trying to optimize every service, or changing Requires when Wants would be safer.

screens.title: What systemd-analyze tells you
screens.narratorSegment: systemd-analyze is the primary command-line tool for measuring and understanding boot performance. At a basic level it reports total boot time and splits that time into kernel and userspace durations. That split is important because kernel delays require a different kind of root cause analysis than userspace delays. The tool's blame subcommand lists all units ordered by the time they consumed during startup, which quickly surfaces long-running services that deserve investigation. The critical-chain subcommand takes a different approach: it shows the chain of dependencies that directly delays reaching the final target. This reveals the critical path — the sequence of units that must complete before your system is considered operational. A practical example: if your database service appears in blame with twenty seconds but critical-chain also shows many services depending on it, optimizing that database startup will reduce overall boot time more than optimizing services not on the critical chain. A common misconception is to optimize every slow service; instead focus on critical-chain entries first. Always pair systemd-analyze results with journalctl logs to see why a unit is slow. How might you prioritize fixes after running these commands?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › What systemd-analyze tells you
Core Concept
Kernel vs userspace times
systemd-analyze reports total boot time and splits kernel and userspace. Use this split to decide where to look: kernel delays suggest drivers, modules, or kernel parameters; userspace delays point to services and init scripts.
Key command
systemd-analyze
This prints total, kernel, and userspace times.
Why it matters
Knowing where the time is spent helps you choose the right diagnostic tools and prevents wasted effort.
Practical example
Imagine systemd-analyze shows kernel time 3.2s and userspace 18.7s. Run blame and critical-chain next. If blame shows a single service at 15s and critical-chain includes that service with many dependents, prioritize that service; if blame shows many 1–2s services but none on critical-chain, parallelization may be sufficient.
Key Takeaway

Measure first. Use kernel vs userspace split to direct your investigation and use critical-chain to focus on the boots' true blockers.

screens.title: Using systemd-analyze blame to find slow services
screens.narratorSegment: systemd-analyze blame lists active units ordered by how long each took to initialize. This command gives you a prioritized suspect list, but the output alone doesn't explain why a unit is slow. When you run blame, look for units taking multiple seconds, then follow up with journalctl -u unitname to see logs during startup. As a concrete example, suppose blame shows mariadb. service at 25s and several other critical services depending on it. Your first step is journalctl -u mariadb. service --since boot to look for timeouts, slow disk input and output, or configuration checks. Next, run systemctl status mariadb. service to see if it's repeatedly failing or being delayed by a TimeoutStartSec. A common error is treating any slow service as worth optimizing; instead, couple blame with critical-chain to see whether speeding that unit will reduce overall boot time. Also remember to run systemd-analyze verify on custom unit files to catch syntax problems that might cause slow starts. In short, blame helps you find suspects; logs and status commands tell you why they're slow. Using systemd-analyze blame to find slow services means run systemd-analyze blame, then inspect each slow unit's logs and status to determine the root cause.. In practical terms, read and interpret blame output to create a prioritized investigation list. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Using systemd-analyze blame
Process Flow
From blame to root cause
Blame gives ordered durations. Use those durations to target investigations with journalctl and systemctl status.
Example command sequence
systemd-analyze blame
journalctl -u mariadb.service --since boot
systemctl status mariadb.service
systemd-analyze verify /etc/systemd/system/myunit.service
Read logs to discover timeouts, I/O waits, or retries during startup.
Common pitfall
Don’t assume every long duration needs optimization. If a unit is not on the critical path, optimizing it may not reduce total boot time.
Concrete example
Suppose blame shows a 25s mariadb.service. journalctl reveals a disk fsck or slow recovery step. Options include tuning database configuration to avoid long recovery on startup, moving data to faster storage, or delaying dependent services until mariadb announces readiness.
Check

After fixing, re-run systemd-analyze blame and critical-chain to confirm reduced boot time.

screens.title: Understanding systemd-analyze critical-chain
screens.narratorSegment: The critical-chain output shows the chain of units that directly delay reaching a target. Unlike blame, which orders by duration, critical-chain shows dependencies and how they accumulate. Each entry includes the time and which unit it depends on. Use critical-chain to spot where one slow unit prevents others from starting, creating a long critical path. For example, if sshd. service depends on networking and mariadb depends on network files, critical-chain may reveal that slow network initialization stretches the entire chain. That tells you to optimize network bring-up or adjust dependency types — maybe change Requires to Wants or reorder After relationships if appropriate. A frequent misconception is to assume all dependencies must be Requires; sometimes using Wants reduces blocking. Always confirm critical-chain findings with logs and with systemctl list-dependencies to see the explicit relationships. When you find the chain, pick the highest-impact candidate for optimization first and re-run the analysis to measure results. Understanding systemd-analyze critical-chain means critical-chain helps you target the dependency sequence that limits how fast the system reaches its final target.. In practical terms, reveal the dependency chain that actually delays boot completion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Understanding critical-chain
Process
Trace the dependency chain
critical-chain lists units that block the boot target. It shows how times accumulate along dependencies so you can find the true bottlenecks.
Example command
systemd-analyze critical-chain
# Inspect chain to find units delaying boot
Use list-dependencies for a structural view and journalctl for unit logs.
Tip
If a unit on the critical path waits for network-online.target, speed network setup or adjust the dependent units to not block unnecessarily.
Key Takeaway

Fix the critical chain first. Shortening units off the chain yields little benefit to total boot time.

screens.title: systemd-bootchart: capture and interpret a boot SVG
screens.narratorSegment: systemd-bootchart produces a visual SVG that shows services as horizontal bars over time, capturing parallel execution, waits, and service durations. To use it, install the systemd-bootchart package, enable its service, and reboot so it records the boot session. The generated SVG typically appears in /run/log/bootchart/ or /var/log/bootchart/. Open it in a browser and look for long bars, gaps where a service is waiting for a dependency, and dense regions where many services hit the disk or network simultaneously. Long horizontal bars are obvious candidates for optimization. Gaps with waiting threads indicate dependency misconfiguration or network/disk waits. A common misreading is to assume any long horizontal bar is always the main cause of slow boot. Always correlate the SVG with systemd-analyze blame and critical-chain, and verify logs for the units involved. Bootchart is invaluable when blame and critical-chain are ambiguous, because it shows concurrency and resource contention visually, making it easier to pick practical fixes. systemd-bootchart: capture and interpret a boot SVG means use bootchart svgs to see parallel execution and resource contention that text outputs can obscure.. In practical terms, how bootchart reveals parallelization, waits, and long-running units. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › systemd-bootchart
Definition
Capture a boot timeline
Bootchart records service execution over time so you can visually inspect parallelism, waits, and service durations.
Install and enable
# RHEL/CentOS/Fedora
sudo dnf install systemd-bootchart
# Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install systemd-bootchart
sudo systemctl enable systemd-bootchart
sudo systemctl start systemd-bootchart
sudo reboot
After reboot, find the SVG in /run/log/bootchart/.
Interpretation cues
  • Long horizontal bars: service startup or blocking operation.
  • Vertical alignment of many bars: disk or CPU contention around the same time window.
  • Gaps with connecting arrows: services waiting for dependencies or network readiness.
Key Takeaway

Combine bootchart visuals with blame and critical-chain to make confident optimization decisions.

screens.title: Common bottlenecks and how to approach them
screens.narratorSegment: When you have identified slow units, approach each candidate with a focused checklist. For long-running services, ask why: is it performing heavy initialization work, waiting on network mounts, or recovering data? Check unit logs, examine application configuration for startup tasks, and consider deferring non-essential work until after the service is marked active. For dependency issues, check whether Requires= is unnecessarily strong; sometimes Wants= or After= is sufficient to avoid blocking. Disk input and output contention often appears when many services access storage simultaneously; apply blkio cgroup limits or stagger startup with systemd's ability to order services. Network availability shows up when services wait for network-online. target; ensure interfaces come up quickly or use systemd-networkd for tighter integration. Use systemd-analyze kernel-config when kernel parameters or modules influence boot. A common mistake is to try to optimize all services; instead use critical-chain to pick high-impact candidates. After applying changes, always test in a staging VM and re-run analysis to confirm improvements. Common bottlenecks and how to approach them means use a checklist per bottleneck type and always re-measure after changes to verify impact.. In practical terms, long-running services, dependencies, disk i/o, and network waits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Common bottlenecks
Comparison
Types of boot bottlenecks
Match the symptom to the likely cause and follow the corresponding remedies to reduce boot time.
Long-running services
Investigate initialization steps, I/O, and network calls. Consider deferring non-critical work.
Dependency issues
Swap Requires for Wants when appropriate and adjust After relations to reduce blocking.
Disk I/O contention
Use IOWeight or cgroup limits and stagger startups to distribute disk load.
Network availability
Ensure interfaces bring up quickly; prefer systemd-networkd for integrated handling and ensure network-online.target is used correctly.
Practical flow
  1. Run systemd-analyze and blame.
  2. Inspect critical-chain and bootchart.
  3. Use journalctl and systemctl status for diagnostics.
  4. Apply targeted fixes, test, and re-measure.
Analogy
Think of boot as a relay race. The critical-chain is the sequence of runners that must all complete. Speeding a runner not on that chain won't shorten the overall finish time.
Common mistake

Trying to optimize every slow unit instead of focusing on the critical path wastes time and risks destabilizing services.

screens.title: Automating post-boot tasks with Type=oneshot
screens.narratorSegment: Automating a post-boot health check or maintenance task is best done with a Type=oneshot systemd service. Type=oneshot services run a command and exit, which is ideal for one-off checks after boot. To ensure they run when prerequisites are ready, set After=multi-user. target and After=network-online. target in the Unit section. If your task depends on a specific service, add After=myservice. service and optionally Requires=myservice. service. A practical example from the chapter demonstrates a health_check. sh placed in /opt/postboot_tasks and a /etc/systemd/system/postboot-health. service that runs it as root and logs to the journal. After creating the unit, run systemctl daemon-reload, enable the service so it runs at boot, and start it to test immediately. Verify execution with systemctl status and journalctl -u. A common pitfall is relying on network. target instead of network-online. target; the latter signals full network availability. Always test in a staging environment and confirm the script exits cleanly so the oneshot service doesn't block other units. Automating post-boot tasks with Type=oneshot means use type=oneshot with after=network-online.target to run scripts once after system startup when network and services are available.. In practical terms, create a reliable oneshot unit that waits for network and required services. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Automating post-boot tasks
Code Walkthrough
Script and unit example
Place a small health-check script and create a Type=oneshot unit that depends on network-online.target to guarantee it runs after the network is ready.
Script (saved as /opt/postboot_tasks/health_check.sh)
#!/bin/bash
LOG_FILE="/var/log/postboot_health.log"
echo "$(date): Starting post-boot health check..." | systemd-cat -t postboot-health
echo "--- System Uptime ---" >> $LOG_FILE
uptime >> $LOG_FILE
echo "--- Network Connectivity (google.com) ---" >> $LOG_FILE
ping -c 3 google.com >> $LOG_FILE 2>&1
if [ $? -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "Network check: SUCCESS" | systemd-cat -t postboot-health
else
  echo "Network check: FAILED" | systemd-cat -t postboot-health -p err
fi
echo "--- Disk Usage ---" >> $LOG_FILE
df -h >> $LOG_FILE
echo "$(date): Post-boot health check complete." | systemd-cat -t postboot-health
Unit file ( /etc/systemd/system/postboot-health.service )
[Unit]
Description=Post-Boot System Health Check
After=multi-user.target network-online.target
# Requires=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/opt/postboot_tasks/health_check.sh
User=root
Group=root
StandardOutput=journal
StandardError=journal

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
Reload systemd and enable the unit with systemctl daemon-reload and systemctl enable postboot-health.service.
Verification
  • systemctl daemon-reload
  • systemctl enable postboot-health.service
  • systemctl start postboot-health.service
  • journalctl -u postboot-health.service -f
Key Takeaway

Use oneshot units with proper After and Requires to run reliable post-boot tasks and validate with journalctl and the log file produced.

Measure → Visualize → Fix → Verify
A step-by-step lab workflow to reproduce in a VM and validate changes safely.
Step 1: Measure
Run systemd-analyze, systemd-analyze blame, and systemd-analyze critical-chain to get baseline timings.
Step 2: Visualize
Enable systemd-bootchart, reboot, and inspect the SVG timeline for parallelism and waits.
Step 3: Hypothesize & Fix
Make small changes: adjust dependency types, add RestartSec, tune cgroup IOWeight, or defer non-critical startup tasks.

Re-run analysis and check journalctl and unit status. Roll back if the change causes regressions.
Real-world check
Always validate fixes in a staging VM and measure the impact; this prevents production outages from configuration errors.

Avoid broad sweeping changes; change one thing at a time so you can attribute improvements to a specific fix.

In this chapter you'll learn practical, hands-on techniques to inspect and improve system startup. We start with systemd-analyze to measure boot time, find slow units with blame, and reveal the critical path with critical-chain. Then you will learn how to capture a visual timeline with systemd-bootchart so you can see which units run in parallel, which block others, and where idle waits occur. Armed with that evidence, you'll practice a targeted troubleshooting workflow: identify suspects, inspect logs, test unit files, and apply dependency and resource changes that shorten the critical path. Finally, you'll automate post-boot activities by writing a Type=oneshot service that runs after multi-user and network-online targets, and learn unit-level best practices like Restart policies, cgroup limits, and pre-flight checks. These techniques let you ensure critical services start reliably, reduce boot time, and automate necessary system health checks. By the end you will be able to both diagnose boot bottlenecks and create dependable automation that runs at the right time during startup.

These objectives frame what you will be able to do after completing the lesson. First, you will use systemd-analyze to inspect boot timing: this means getting kernel and userspace times, running blame to list slow services, and using critical-chain to see the critical path. Knowing which unit lives on the critical path lets you focus where it matters. Second, you will generate and interpret a systemd-bootchart SVG so you can visually correlate long horizontal bars with services and see parallel versus blocked work. Third, you will learn to identify and resolve common bottlenecks such as long-running services, dependency misconfiguration, disk input and output contention, and slow network bring-up. Fourth, you will automate post-boot scripts using Type=oneshot units and targets like network-online. target so tasks run only when prerequisites are satisfied. Each objective ties to a competency milestone so you can verify your work with systemctl, journalctl, and bootchart inspection.

We continue with verification and resilience objectives that ensure your optimizations are safe. You will use systemd-analyze verify to check custom unit syntax before you enable units widely, catching errors early and avoiding boot-time failures caused by misconfigured unit files. You will also design unit files that increase service reliability: learning when to use Restart policies such as on-failure, how to add RestartSec to avoid tight restart loops, and when to apply cgroup resource limits like MemoryMax to protect system stability. Finally, you will practice target and dependency choices: deciding between Requires and Wants, and using After and Before to control order without creating unnecessary blocking. Each objective includes a verification step — check logs with journalctl, validate unit state with systemctl status, and test changes in a staging VM before production. This practice helps you avoid common mistakes: trying to optimize every service, or changing Requires when Wants would be safer.

systemd-analyze is the primary command-line tool for measuring and understanding boot performance. At a basic level it reports total boot time and splits that time into kernel and userspace durations. That split is important because kernel delays require a different kind of root cause analysis than userspace delays. The tool's blame subcommand lists all units ordered by the time they consumed during startup, which quickly surfaces long-running services that deserve investigation. The critical-chain subcommand takes a different approach: it shows the chain of dependencies that directly delays reaching the final target. This reveals the critical path — the sequence of units that must complete before your system is considered operational. A practical example: if your database service appears in blame with twenty seconds but critical-chain also shows many services depending on it, optimizing that database startup will reduce overall boot time more than optimizing services not on the critical chain. A common misconception is to optimize every slow service; instead focus on critical-chain entries first. Always pair systemd-analyze results with journalctl logs to see why a unit is slow. How might you prioritize fixes after running these commands?

systemd-analyze blame lists active units ordered by how long each took to initialize. This command gives you a prioritized suspect list, but the output alone doesn't explain why a unit is slow. When you run blame, look for units taking multiple seconds, then follow up with journalctl -u unitname to see logs during startup. As a concrete example, suppose blame shows mariadb. service at 25s and several other critical services depending on it. Your first step is journalctl -u mariadb. service --since boot to look for timeouts, slow disk input and output, or configuration checks. Next, run systemctl status mariadb. service to see if it's repeatedly failing or being delayed by a TimeoutStartSec. A common error is treating any slow service as worth optimizing; instead, couple blame with critical-chain to see whether speeding that unit will reduce overall boot time. Also remember to run systemd-analyze verify on custom unit files to catch syntax problems that might cause slow starts. The critical-chain output shows the chain of units that directly delay reaching a target. Unlike blame, which orders by duration, critical-chain shows dependencies and how they accumulate. Each entry includes the time and which unit it depends on. Use critical-chain to spot where one slow unit prevents others from starting, creating a long critical path.
